title: The Impossible Harbor
premise: Paloma Sandoval, a once-celebrated cellist whose hands froze mid-concert in front of a thousand people, retreats to the island town of Gullwrack Harbor to teach music and avoid feeling anything at all. When his estranged family descends for his grandmother's eightieth birthday reunion, he hires Marisol Vega — the ferry mechanic who once fixed his broken bow case and never let him forget it — to pose as his partner for one weekend. The lie curdles into truth over three days of shared rooms, old wounds, and a grandmother who sees through everything, forcing Paloma to confront that his stage collapse was really a collapse of self-worth. At the season's last ferry, with Marisol boarding to leave him behind as he once left music, he plays cello on the dock — badly, publicly, joyfully — and chooses love and imperfection over the safe silence he'd mistaken for control.
about_author: Noor Underhill is a former orchestra librarian who spent a decade backstage watching brilliant musicians quietly fall apart, an obsession that fuels her tender, music-soaked romances. She lives on a cold coast with a rescue dog named Fermata and writes only during ferry crossings.

chapters.title: The Muscle That Forgets
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Eight months after his catastrophic final performance, Paloma teaches cello to indifferent teenagers in Gullwrack Harbor and insists aloud that the heart is trainable, containable. A letter summons him to his grandmother's eightieth-birthday reunion — where his ex-fiancée will attend. Emotional beat: brittle denial cracking at the edges.

chapters.title: Ferry Mechanics
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol, who grew up on the island and knows everyone's business, repairs Paloma's waterlogged bow case and teases out his panic about the reunion. On impulse he asks her to be his fake girlfriend; she names a price: honesty by dessert, no exceptions. Emotional beat: wary spark disguised as a transaction.

chapters.title: Rules of Engagement
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. They draft absurd rules over chowder — hand-holding permitted, backstories off-limits — while rehearsing each other's details like sheet music. Paloma realizes he can perform intimacy more easily than real conversation. Emotional beat: comic warmth shadowed by his fear of being truly known.

chapters.title: Arrivals
chapters.summary: Dual POV. The family converges: Paloma's disapproving brother Tomás, his polished ex-fiancée Camille, and Abuela Rosa, sharp-eyed and delighted by Marisol. The first dinner goes suspiciously well until someone asks how they met, and Marisol improvises a story too true to be a lie. Emotional beat: the fake begins bleeding into the real.

chapters.title: What the Grandmother Knows
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Rosa corners Marisol in the kitchen, reveals she recognized the arrangement within minutes, and asks instead what Marisol wants for herself — a question Marisol has dodged her whole rootless life. Meanwhile Paloma overhears Camille say he was always 'easier when he wasn't playing.' Emotional beat: longing sharpened by recognition.

chapters.title: Duet in a Locked Room
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Trapped together by a storm during the reunion talent night, Paloma and Marisol hide in the boathouse, where he confesses the truth of his collapse: not stage fright, but shame — his father's voice in his head calling music a waste. She tells him her own secret: she never stays anywhere longer than a season. Emotional beat: raw mutual confession, almost-kiss interrupted.

chapters.title: The Wrong Kind of Real
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. The kiss finally happens — and then Tomás exposes the fake-dating arrangement at breakfast, weaponizing it against Paloma. Humiliated, Paloma pushes Marisol away with cruel precision, insisting none of it was ever real. Emotional beat: heartbreak; both retreat into their oldest defenses.

chapters.title: Broken Strings
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Wrecked, Paloma finds Rosa packing away his childhood cello and delivers the novel's turn: she tells him forgiveness isn't earned from others but granted to yourself, and that his father's cruelty was fear wearing armor. He picks up the instrument for the first time in a year. Emotional beat: grief transmuting into acceptance.

chapters.title: Last Ferry of the Season
chapters.summary: Dual POV. The reunion ends; Marisol boards the final autumn ferry, having decided staying means risking the leaving she's always chosen first. Paloma races to the dock carrying his cello and his whole unguarded self. Emotional beat: climax — the choice between safety and love made public and irreversible.

chapters.title: Everything Out of Tune
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, epilogue in spring. Paloma plays on the dock — imperfect, audible, alive — and Marisol misses the ferry on purpose. Months later they run a summer music school together; his family returns, awkward and trying; the heart, it turns out, was never containable. Emotional beat: belonging found, joyfully unresolved into ongoing life.
